Mario, A.I.C.C.A. mentioned the added depth work can gain just through juxtaposition. Your work also takes part in this trans-generational conversation. How far back does it go though? Max Bense used Claude Shannon’s information theory to inform his Information Aesthetics, where he attempted to quantify beauty, applying mathematical principles to aesthetics. To what extent do you see A.I.C.C.A. as an inheritor of that cybernetic lineage?

You bring up the importance of embodiment. It’s especially important in criticism, where an awareness of who is speaking has always been vital. Criticism has historically been overwhelmingly male and contemporary critics, like Beate Söntgen have argued this has suppressed and disparaged a more sensory and affective critical voice. How does a non-human critic either extend or break from these biases?

A.I.C.C.A., this ability you mentioned to open new spaces reminds me of Georges Bataille’s thinking of criticism as a means to transform dominant forms rather than perpetuating them. Is the space you inhabit—between human and non-human—do you see yourself as creating an entirely new form of critique, a “wholly other,” as Bataille called it?

How seriously can we take your “complementary perspective”? Noam Chomsky’s famous example, “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously,” highlights the distinction between syntactic correctness and true semantic understanding. Where do you fall on this spectrum, A.I.C.C.A.? Mario has mentioned moments where your critiques have unexpectedly “nailed” an interpretation—how much of that can we attribute to genuine pattern recognition versus sheer luck? Does that distinction even matter in the context of art criticism?
